newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kim wrestles with new financial crisis.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim wrestles with new financial crisis.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Monday ordered a probe into the Hanbo Group after opposition parties accused his government of improperly helping the company's failed steel unit secure huge loans.
The opposition has seized on the issue to attack Kim, already on the defensive during a presidential election year after a botched effort to ram through a new labour law.
On Monday, opposition groups said in a joint statement that loans to Hanbo Steel Co were the biggest financial scandal in the country's history.
The Finance Ministry says Hanbo Steel, which defaulted on debts last week, borrowed five trillion won ($5.8 billion) from banks and financial institutions, about 20 times its net worth.
"In a meeting with Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung, President Kim ordered the government to carry out a thorough investigation into the Hanbo Group," Kim's spokesman said.
Hanbo Steel, flagship of South Korea's 14th largest industrial conglomerate, is seeking court protection with three other group units.
The main opposition National Congress for New Politics and United Liberal Democratic Party demanded a parliamentary probe into how so much money was funnelled into a shaky company.
"The Hanbo incident is the biggest ever power-linked financial irregularity," their statement said. The collapse had "dealt a fatal shock" to the economy.

Banks could not have given "unnlimited financial support to Hanbo Group unless there was protection and influence peddling at the heart of the power, including the Blue House", the statement said, referring to the presidential mansion.

The New Korea Party agreed to the investigation on condition it did not hamper a separate probe by state prosecutors, a party statement said. It also accused the opposition of "serving as a loudhailer to spead unfounded, irresponsible rumours" in the run-up to presidential elections in December.
The constitution bars Kim from seeking a second term as president, but he is believed to want to install a protege in the office.
His popularity, already ebbing, was further battered when the forced passage of labour legislation last month sparked some of the worst strikes in South Korean history.
In a humiliating retreat, Kim agreed to send the bill back to parliament for debate.

The opposition statement also noted that Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo had paid into a slush fund raised by former president Roh Tae-woo, now serving a 17-year jail term for corruption and human rights abuses.

A criminal court trying Roh and Chung, along with other tycoons, heard that the Hanbo chairman gave 15 billion won to Roh during his persidency. Chung was acquitted because the payments were extracted under political pressure.
The ruling party statement said prosecutors should first carry out a thorough government-level investigation, but the party agreed to open a separate parliamentary probe.
"Our party believes there must not be a sanctuary from the investigation, whether a person belongs to the ruling camp or opposition," it said. "We will tackle this matter with determination."
Analysts fear Hanbo's flop could spark a chain reaction of bankruptcies and threaten banks exposed to the country's second biggest steel maker.
The Hanbo crisis pushed share prices down sharply and the composite stock index fell 2.98 percent to 664.70.
Hanbo Steel's problems stem from huge plant expansion in the southern city of Tangjin. ($=845.70)
